On pages 413 to 414 the book says that because packets go to a failed router "the packets will be sent to the other router". That sentence is muddled. What really happens is: the packets keep going to the dead router's MAC address until the ARP entry expires, and only then does the other router answer. Failover is slow because it depends on the ARP timeout.
ARP timeouts differ by operating system.
Proxy ARP was not designed as a gateway redundancy tool, and many designs turn it off.
General knowledge, not verified in this session.
This slow, accidental failover is the problem FHRPs solve. They give the host one gateway that never changes and fail over in seconds or less.
Why does the host not learn about the failure of its gateway?
Routers update each other, not the hosts - hosts have a single configured gateway and usually do not run routing.
In Proxy ARP, whose MAC address does the router give to the host?
The router's own MAC address - the host thinks it is the MAC of the destination.
What decides how long a host keeps sending to a dead Proxy ARP router?
The ARP cache timeout on the host - the old entry must age out before a new ARP request is sent.

Which FHRP gives true load balancing?
GLBP - HSRP and VRRP use one forwarding router per group.
Why is failover transparent to hosts?
The standby router takes over the same virtual IP and MAC - the host's gateway setting and ARP entry stay valid.

Very short timers on a busy or unstable network can cause the active role to flap. Test any change.
What are the default HSRP hello and hold times?
3 seconds and 10 seconds - the hold time is about three times the hello time.
Which timer makes the standby router decide the active router is gone?
The hold timer - it counts the time without a Hello from the active router.
To use millisecond timers that all routers learn, which HSRP version do you need?
Version 2 - version 1 does not advertise or learn millisecond timers.
